Here is a verse-by-verse commentary on Psalm 28, drawing on the sources I could access within the constraints.

## Psalm 28 — Verse-by-Verse Notes

### Overview / Structure

Psalm 28 is "A Psalm of David." The psalm falls into two clear halves: **vv. 1–5 are lament/petition**, and **vv. 6–9 are thanksgiving/praise** (Constable, Spurgeon). David Guzik calls it "Praise from Prayer Heard and Answered." Spurgeon sees the main pleading as the suppliant asking not to be confounded with the workers of iniquity, and he notes: "The Lord Jesus may be seen here pleading as the representative of his people." The psalm moves from urgent private prayer to corporate intercession for all God's people — a movement that, Guzik notes, reflects what happens when we draw near to the Lord.

— Spurgeon: https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps028.php  
— Guzik: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-28/

### v. 1 — "To You, O LORD, I call; be not deaf to me, O my Rock. For if You remain silent, I will become like those descending to the Pit."

**Traditional reading:** David opens with a determined cry. Gill notes that the phrase "Unto thee will I cry" shows fervency, resolution, and a commitment to direct all appeals to the Lord alone. The title "my Rock" (Hebrew *tsûr*) speaks of solidity, strength, and refuge — David clings to God as his only firm foundation. Ellicott explains that *tsûr* comes from a root meaning "bind together," indicating strength and solidity; "rock" was a common metaphor for a tutelary deity adopted for Jehovah throughout the Psalms.

The plea "be not silent to me" (or "be not deaf to me") reflects the psalmist's urgent situation. Spurgeon writes: "Mere formalists may be content without answers to their prayers, but genuine suppliants cannot; they are not satisfied with the results of prayer itself in calming the mind and subduing the will — they must go further and obtain actual replies from heaven, or they cannot rest." Guzik adds that David felt God was silent to him but in faith gave God the title he longed for Him to fulfill: his Rock.

"If You remain silent… I become like those going down to the Pit" — Ellicott says the *pit* (*bôr*) is either the sepulchre or the world of the dead, suggesting the psalmist was on a bed of sickness. Guzik and Kidner note that the fear is not dread of death as such, but of death with unmerited disgrace — being lumped together with the wicked. Pulpit Commentary adds: "i.e. without hope, desperate."

### v. 2 — "Hear my cry for mercy when I call to You for help, when I lift up my hands toward Your holy sanctuary."

**Traditional reading:** This verse intensifies the plea through repetition and bodily posture. "Lifting up the hands" was the usual Hebrew prayer posture, signifying utter dependence on God (Constable). The Pulpit Commentary explains that originally the idea was hands ready to receive God's blessings, but later it symbolised lifting up the heart (citing Lamentations 3:41). Spurgeon says: "We stretch out empty hands, for we are beggars; we lift them up, for we seek heavenly supplies; we lift them towards the mercy seat of Jesus, for there our expectation dwells."

The "holy sanctuary" (or "holy oracle," Hebrew *debir*) refers to the innermost sanctuary — the Holy of Holies where the ark rested, the place from which God spoke. Gill notes this is a type of Christ, the true Oracle through whom God speaks. Guzik addresses the suggestion that this reference to a "sanctuary" proves a later (post-Davidic) date: he notes, with Kidner, that the tabernacle was also a holy sanctuary and the term may have been in use well before Solomon's temple.

### v. 3 — "Do not drag me away with the wicked, and with the workers of iniquity, who speak peace to their neighbors while malice is in their hearts."

**Traditional reading:** The petition is that David not share the fate of the wicked. The verb "drag me away" (or "draw me not away") uses the metaphor of a hunter drawing prey into a net (Pulpit) or of prisoners being dragged to execution (Spurgeon: "like felons of old drawn on a hurdle to Tyburn, like logs drawn to the fire"). Ellicott references Ezekiel 32:18ff, where wicked nations are dragged to destruction.

The wicked are characterised by **false speech**: "they speak peace to their neighbours, but mischief is in their hearts." Spurgeon calls this "the deceitful meshes of the infernal net in which Satan catches the precious life," noting that soft, oily words disguise deadly intent. Gill applies this to hypocrites "who have a form of godliness, but deny the power of it." The Pulpit Commentary points to biblical examples of such treachery: Joab killing Abner (2 Samuel 3:27) and Amasa (2 Samuel 20:9–10).

— Pulpit: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/28.htm  
— Spurgeon: https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps028.php

### v. 4 — "Repay them according to their deeds and for their works of evil. Repay them for what their hands have done; bring back on them what they deserve."

**Traditional reading:** This is one of the so-called **imprecatory** passages in the Psalms. Four parallel phrases hammer the point: *according to their deeds*, *the wickedness of their endeavours*, *the work of their hands*, *what they deserve*.

**How traditions differ on this verse:**

- **Spurgeon (Baptist/Reformed):** Opens an extended discussion, acknowledging the difficulty. He suggests that viewing the words as *prophetic declaration* (future tense) rather than personal vindictiveness is "nearer to the true meaning." God takes the will for the deed: "Our endeavours are taken as facts; God takes the will for the deed, and punishes or rewards accordingly." Yet he admits the desires in this verse "are not readily made consistent with the spirit of the Christian dispensation, which seeks rather the reformation than the punishment of sinners." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps028.php)

- **Gill (Reformed Baptist):** Defends the prayer as not contrary to Christian charity: "Such petitions are not contrary to that Christian charity which the Gospel recommends; nor do they savour of a spirit of revenge." He argues the psalmist spoke "by a prophetic spirit, knowing what was the will of God in this case," and that these petitions "are not to be drawn into an example in common and ordinary cases." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/28.htm)

- **Ellicott (Anglican):** Says there is "no indication of personal animosity or vindictiveness." The poet was "identified with devout Israel," and it was natural to pray that God would "vindicate Himself and justify those faithful to Him." He notes that the *lex talionis* (law of exact retribution) was "deeply impressed on the mind of Israel." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/28.htm)

- **Pulpit Commentary (Anglican/ecumenical):** Grounds the prayer in the natural moral sense: "The feeling of righteous indignation, naturally implanted in us, causes us to desire the punishment of the wicked, quite apart from any wrong that they may have done to ourselves." It adds: "Nothing satisfies our moral feelings but exact retribution." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/28.htm)

- **Guzik (Charismatic/Evangelical):** Notes David's approach contrasts with how he prayed for himself: in his own sin, David cast himself on mercy; for the unrepentant wicked, he prayed for harsh judgment. Kidner (quoted by Guzik) says: "These verses are not simply vindictive, but put into words the protest of any healthy conscience at the wrongs of the present order, and the conviction that a day of judgment is a moral necessity." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-28/)

- **Matthew Henry (Puritan/Reformed):** Takes the prayer as a model of hating sin while loving sinners, though the full text was not accessible in this research.

### v. 5 — "Since they show no regard for the works of the LORD or what His hands have done, He will tear them down and never rebuild them."

**Traditional reading:** The root sin of the wicked is identified: they ignore God's works — in creation, providence, and redemption. The Pulpit Commentary says: "They do not note God's providential workings. If they did, they would see that judgment falls upon the wicked… God is not in all their thoughts." Guzik connects this to Romans 1:20–21: the wicked are "without excuse" because creation plainly reveals God.

"He will tear them down and never rebuild them" — the destruction is total and irreversible. Gill calls it "everlasting destruction." The Pulpit Commentary notes the contrast: God builds up the righteous but tears down the wicked permanently. The Preacher's Complete Homiletical Commentary says the verse shows that "God will seem to men according to what they are."

### v. 6 — "Blessed be the LORD, for He has heard my cry for mercy."

**Traditional reading:** This verse marks the dramatic turning point of the psalm. Spurgeon writes: "They who pray well, will soon praise well: prayer and praise are the two lips of the soul." He calls them "two young roes that are twins, feeding upon the mountain of myrrh."

There is a long-standing debate about what happened between v. 5 and v. 6. Ellicott notes three scholarly theories: (1) an interval of time elapsed during which the answer came; (2) the psalm combines two originally separate pieces; (3) v. 6 is an interpolation. However, the traditional reading, represented by Spurgeon, Guzik, and Gill, is that David's faith *anticipated* the answer — he believed he had received what he asked. As Guzik puts it: "Real praise is established upon sufficient and constraining reasons; it is not irrational emotion, but rises, like a pure spring, from the deeps of experience" (quoting Spurgeon). Gill notes that some Jewish commentators (Aben Ezra, Kimchi) understand this "in a way of prophecy" — David spoke by faith, assured of the answer. The Expositor's Bible Commentary says: "As in many psalms, the faith which prays passes at once into the faith which possesses."

— Spurgeon: https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps028.php  
— Ellicott: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/28.htm  
— Guzik: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-28/  
— Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/28.htm

### v. 7 — "The LORD is my strength and my shield; my heart trusts in Him, and I am helped. Therefore my heart rejoices, and I give thanks to Him with my song."

**Traditional reading:** This is the great confession of trust vindicated. "The Lord is my strength" means God does not merely *give* strength — He *is* strength to the believer (Guzik). Spurgeon exults: "My dear friend, if you can say, 'The Lord is my strength,' you can bear anything and everything. You could bear a martyr's death if the Lord should be your strength." Gill distinguishes: God is the author of both natural and spiritual strength — strength of body, fortitude of mind, strength in life and in the hour of death.

"My heart trusted in Him, and I am helped" — the order is crucial: trust precedes help. Spurgeon says: "Heart work is sure work; heart trust is never disappointed. Faith must come before help, but help will never be long behindhand." The word "heart" appears twice in this verse, underscoring the sincerity of both trust and joy.

"Therefore my heart greatly rejoices" — Ellicott suggests the better translation is "danceth for joy" (as in the Prayer Book). The rejoicing is exuberant, bodily, expressed in song.

**Baptist/Piper note:** John Piper (Desiring God) references Psalm 28:7 when discussing how believers find renewed strength: "The Lord is my strength and my shield; in him my heart trusts, and I am helped." He says: "So the Lord himself is our strength, and the psalmist says that we experience that strength by trusting in him." He also links this to Nehemiah 8:10: "The joy of the Lord is your strength." This reflects a characteristic Reformed-Baptist emphasis on faith as the instrument by which God's strength is received. (https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/strategies-for-when-life-seems-aimless)

### v. 8 — "The LORD is the strength of His people, a stronghold of salvation for His anointed."

**Traditional reading:** The psalm now widens from individual to corporate. What God is to David, He is to all His people. Spurgeon says: "The heavenly experience of one believer is a pattern of the life of all." The phrase "His anointed" (*mashiach*) operates on two levels: (1) David himself as the anointed king, and (2) typologically, the ultimate Anointed One — Jesus Christ. Gill explicitly reads it of the Messiah: "the Lord's Anointed, whom he heard, helped, and strengthened in the day of salvation, and delivered him from the power of death and the grave." Guzik similarly notes: "His anointed ones are secure in the Messiah, and therefore strong and safe."

**Ellicott's critical note:** The LXX and Vulgate read "to his people" rather than "their strength," harmonising with Psalm 29:11. This reflects a textual variant noted in the manuscript tradition. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/28.htm)

— Spurgeon: https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps028.php  
— Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/28.htm  
— Guzik: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-28/

### v. 9 — "Save Your people and bless Your inheritance; shepherd them and carry them forever."

**Traditional reading:** Four short petitions close the psalm — **save, bless, shepherd, carry/lift up**. Guzik calls these petitions that "each address a specific need of God's people."

- **Save** — deliverance from enemies, sin, and trouble. Gill calls it a prayer of faith, since God has already resolved to save His people.
- **Bless** — positive bestowal of spiritual and material good. God's people are His "inheritance," His treasured possession.
- **Shepherd** — the Hebrew *ra'ah* means both "feed" and "govern" (Clarke, cited by Guzik). God is to care for His people as a shepherd tends his flock (cf. Psalm 23).
- **Carry them / lift them up forever** — the Pulpit Commentary notes two interpretations: (a) carrying in His arms like a shepherd carries lambs (a continuation of the shepherd metaphor; Kay, *Speaker's Commentary*), or (b) "exalt, lift up on high, raise above others" (preferred by Horsley, Rosenmüller, and Hengstenberg). Spurgeon combines both: "Carry them in thine arms on earth, and then lift them into thy bosom in heaven."

Guzik, quoting F.B. Meyer, captures the movement of the whole psalm: "When you are nearest the Lord, you are almost certain to begin pleading for his inheritance." The psalm begins with a cry for personal deliverance and ends with intercession for all God's people.

**Messianic/Christological note:** Spurgeon, Gill, and Guzik all see Christ foreshadowed. Spurgeon says: "Here behold king David as the type of our Lord Jesus, our covenant Head, our anointed Prince, through whom all blessings come to us."

— Spurgeon: https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps028.php

— Guzik: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-28/

## Summary of Key Tradition-Specific Differences

| Issue | Traditions |
|---|---|
| **v. 4 — The imprecation** | **Reformed/Spurgeon**: Prefer to read as prophetic declaration, not personal vengeance; acknowledge tension with NT ethics. **Gill (Reformed Baptist)**: Defends as non-vindictive, spoken by prophetic spirit, not an example for ordinary cases. **Anglican (Ellicott, Pulpit)**: No personal animosity; reflects Israel's concern for God's honour and the *lex talionis*. **Charismatic/Evangelical (Guzik)**: A "moral necessity" — protest of a healthy conscience against wrong. |
| **v. 6 — The sudden shift** | **Traditional (Spurgeon, Gill, Guzik)**: Faith anticipates the answer; prayer passes into praise through assurance. **Critical/Anglican (Ellicott)**: Notes scholarly theories of separate compositions or interpolation, though does not endorse them. |
| **v. 8 — "His anointed"** | **Messianic (Gill, Spurgeon, Guzik)**: Reads Christologically — the ultimate Anointed One. **Historical-critical (Ellicott)**: The writer was a king (David), referring to himself and his dynasty. Both readings can coexist in traditional interpretation. |
| **v. 9 — "lift them up"** | **Shepherd metaphor school (Kay, Speaker's Commentary)**: Carrying lambs. **Exaltation school (Horsley, Hengstenberg)**: Lifting up in honour/glory. **Spurgeon**: Holds both together — carried now, exalted eternally. |
